title: 23 Lessons I Learned From Robert Greene On Life, Work, and The Sublime

content:
By the way you can come see me in Bastrop (today with Matthew McConaughey) and then next week in Nashville…then in Philly and DC in December!

Almost twenty years ago, when I was 19 years old, I found myself sitting across from a person who would teach me more than just about any single person I have ever known.

It was at The Alcove in Los Feliz and the great Robert Greene was talking to another author about all the trouble he was having finding a good research assistant. I had to restrain myself from jumping over the table. This was literally my dream job. It was what I wanted to do with my life.

Fortunately, before I made a fool of myself, Robert asked if I might have any interest in giving it a shot. It didn’t start with anything glamorous. In the days before AI or even decent software, I spent hours transcribing interviews he had done for a book he was writing. I read obscure books. I found articles. I worked on his website. I went to libraries and scanned pages. I went through old archives. I tracked people down.

And in between, I asked questions. I listened. I watched. I absorbed his research and note card system, which I continue to use to this day. I got to see up close what it takes to do great work. Robert was a generous boss and he paid me well, but the real compensation for the job was that I got to have regular conversations with him. And the real luck of my life has been that those conversations continued after my time as his assistant ended (he’s been on the Daily Stoic podcast here, here, here and here). He’s the person I call when I need advice or am struggling with something. He remains one of my favorite writers ever.

So in honor of his new book, The Law of the Sublime—which is incredible and everyone should read right now—I thought I’d share some of the best things I have learned from this incredible man.

– Value learning over money. I told Robert I would work for him for free. “Nobody,” he said firmly, “works for me for free.” In fact, he would often have to nag me to submit my hours. To me, the money was an afterthought. I always considered having access to him, getting to ask him questions, getting to see how a real pro did the job, as my actual compensation. What would he have normally charged someone as a consultant? How many people would have killed to be able to call him or email him about anything?  “Value learning over money,” as Robert writes in Mastery. Always go to what will teach you the most, not what will pay the most. “In the end,” Robert continues, “by valuing learning above all else, you will set the stage for your creative expansion, and the money will soon come to you.”

– Seize the alive time. When I was thinking about leaving my job at American Apparel to be a writer, Robert took me to lunch. It was kind of a full-circle moment from our first meeting. Encouraging me to take the leap in a year or so, he explained there were two types of time in life: Alive time and Dead time. One is when you sit around, when you wait until things happen to you. The other is when you are using that time productively, actively. You’re stuck at the airport–you don’t control that. You decide whether it’s alive time or dead time (you read a book, you take a walk, you call your grandmother). How was I going to use the next year? What would I have to show for it? Don’t just sit on your hands. Decide: This is an opportunity for me. I am using it for my purposes. I will not let this be dead time for me. It was an incredibly productive period of reading and researching and filling boxes of notecards that helped me write The Obstacle is the Way and Ego is the Enemy.

– Be involved. One of the things I’ve always admired about Robert is that he gets involved. When I met him, he was on the board of directors of American Apparel. Over the years, I’ve seen the different politicians, political movements, and causes he’s supported. He uses his powers to contribute, to change the world. He understands how things work, and he puts that understanding to use.

– Never lose your heart. People think Robert is dark and Machiavellian because of what he writes about. But my own political sense of the world was shaped in part by Robert: here is someone who understands the amorality of history and still has a strong social conscience. It’s funny—people assume that because of his books, he must be super conservative. In fact, he’s not. Nothing brings me joy quite like seeing people on Instagram call us both “libtards.”

– Greatness takes time. Robert worked on The Law of the Sublime for the last seven years. He always takes a long time on his books, but I don’t think he wanted this one to take that long. Because of his stroke, he had to do all of the work by hand. But I’ve never once seen him allow anyone to rush him. He always goes at the pace it needs to take. I think about that when I feel behind schedule. It takes what it takes.

– Be useful—and pay attention while you’re doing it. Some of my earliest work for Robert involved transcribing interviews. I would listen, stop the recording, type, go back, listen again. In our recent conversation, we talked about how easily that work can now be automated. But I also told him what those hours had given me. I got to listen to people who would never have agreed to be interviewed by me. I got to hear how Robert asked questions, what he pursued, how he drew things out of people. There was an education inside the assignment. Robert explained that a good apprentice makes a mentor’s life easier. You figure out what they need. You take something off their plate. You develop a skill that complements theirs. That’s how you earn access. What you do with that access is up to you. You can complete the task and collect the money. You can also study how a person you admire thinks and works. The second part is what stays with you long after the assignment is over.

– Develop your intuition. Robert has this incredible ability to sense where to find the story he needs. He’ll be working on a chapter, trying to illustrate a particular idea, and have a hunch that the perfect example is somewhere in a certain book or biography. He hasn’t found it yet. He can’t point you to the passage. But he suspects that if he digs into that book, he’ll find what he’s looking for. And so often, he’s right. I remember asking about it once, and he said, “I’m like a shark,” able to detect the faintest scent of blood across the vast ocean of information. It’s an incredible intuition he’s developed through decades of reading and researching. He knows so much about history, about different eras, about people, about every school of thought, that he has for books and ideas and stories that Fingerspitzengefühl (fingertip feel) he writes about in The 33 Strategies of War—the instinctive sense of where to go that comes from a “deep knowledge of the terrain.”

– Never settle for mediocre.  Robert’s rigor as a reader and researcher was legendary. When I was working with him on The 50th Law, I saw him decide that the book was going in the wrong direction, toss what he had, and start over.  As his research assistant, he would send me off to find stories for his writing. He taught me to hold what I read—and what I brought him—to a very high standard. Finding the perfect quote or story for whatever he was working on wasn’t enough. Where did it come from? What was the context? Was the source itself legitimate? Does it hold up across other sources? Was I settling for the first thing that seemed relevant or confirmed what I wanted? I see too many books these days that skip over all of those questions. They’re filled with lazy writing and research. Quotes clearly pulled from some quote aggregator website. The same handful of familiar stories. Lines attributed to someone without any indication of where they said it—“As Mark Twain said…” Did he? Where? What was the context? Don’t settle for the first thing that sort of fits. Keep digging. For a better source, a stronger example, a more thoroughly verified quote. Set high standards, then do the work to meet them.

– Be patient. In 2009, I wrote an article about stoicism on Tim Ferriss’s website. This was probably my biggest stage as a writer at that point—and then a few months later, a small publisher emailed me to ask if I wanted to turn that article into a book. It was as if everything I had hoped for was coming together. But I wanted to check with Robert first—did he think I should do it? He told me he was happy for me but actually suggested I turn the book offer down. He said that I was still learning and improving as a writer—that my life experiences were accelerating and that the book would be better each day I waited. He was teaching me to be patient. It’s easier to be patient when nothing is happening though. To turn down a life-changing opportunity? That’s the real test. And he was right. If I had taken the deal I had gotten offered in 2009, my entire life would have been different.

– Concentrate your forces. You can’t do a million things well. Robert mostly just writes, and that’s rare these days. Authors are consultants. Authors are starting apps. There are all these other things we can do. For the last seven years, Robert did almost no speaking. He was writing. I think about that example a lot. The reason Robert is as good as he is is that he follows one of his own laws from The 48 Laws of Power: concentrate your forces.

– Don’t outsource the thinking process. A little while back, I asked Robert what he thought about AI. “I think back to when I was 19-years-old and in college,” Robert said. In a class learning to read and translate classical Greek texts, “They gave us a passage of Thucydides, the hardest writer of all to read in ancient Greek. I had this one paragraph I must have spent ten hours trying to translate…That had an incredible impact on me. It developed character, patience, and discipline that helps me even to this day. What if I had ChatGPT, and I put the passage in there, and it gave me the translation right away? The whole thinking process would have been annihilated right there.” This is why I—as I learned from Robert—do all my research on physical notecards. It is not fast, easy, or efficient. And that is the point. Writing things down by hand forces me to engage and struggle with the material for an extended period of time. It forces me to take my time. To go over things again and again. To be immersed. To be focused, patient, and disciplined. To come to understand things deeply.

– Creativity is a lagging indicator. Robert’s definition of creativity is this: “creativity is a function of the previous work you put in.” Creativity is not mysterious or romantic. It’s tedious, Robert says. “If you put a lot of hours into thinking and researching and reading, hour after hour—a very tedious process—creativity will come to you.” All of my books are lagging indicators. They are a culmination of years of work. This is what keeps me moving—knowing that I have to keep filling and refilling the creative well. Knowing that creative output is a lagging indicator of a lot of hours of tedious work. Knowing that if I want to publish more books in the future, the only question is, am I doing the work now?

– Make your way to the inside. Robert’s metaphor for mastery is being on the inside of something. When we start a new sport, when we get our first job, when we approach a field we haven’t yet studied, we are on the outside. But as we put in the work, as we familiarize ourselves with every component, as we develop our intuitive field, we eventually make our way to the inside. This is a metaphor from Robert I think about constantly. I don’t want to be an outsider on anything I do, I want to make my way inside it.

– Focus, focus, focus. If you call Robert in the middle of the day, he won’t answer. Because he’s working. That might seem like a minor accomplishment, but any writer knows how much discipline that takes. You’re sitting there, the words aren’t coming and you’re begging for any excuse to stop. Robert’s discipline is an inspiration for me and I use it as a model. I don’t often meet it, but I try. I remember once I was with Robert when my phone made a noise and I immediately picked it up to check what it was. He compared the way I instinctively reached for it to a “rat in an experiment.” There’s a reason I have turned off all alerts on my phone. I’m still not nearly as indistractable as Robert is, but I’m far better than I would have been without his example.

– Be loyal to the truth. I once asked Robert about what I think is the thread through all his books, something which is also in short supply these days: an unflinching commitment to reality, even when it’s inconvenient. “Whenever I hold a belief, or I’m writing a book,” Robert explained, “I always start with the premise that I’m probably wrong, that I’m actually quite ignorant, that my idea is pretty stupid. And I look at the evidence on the other side and I examine it and I try to convince myself that my initial idea was right. And if it isn’t, then I change it.”

– Separate understanding from endorsing. People often assume the author of The 48 Laws of Power must be a sinister person. But beneath his Machiavellian reputation, there was kindness, patience, decency, generosity, wisdom. One of the lessons I took from this was to separate understanding a behavior from endorsing it. You need to recognize manipulation, vanity, and ambition. You also need to decide how you will behave.

– Take your work seriously…but never yourself. Again, continuing on the idea of understanding vs. endorsing, people think because Robert’s work is very serious that he must be as well. In fact, he’s hilarious. That’s why I loved his interview on Pete Holmes’ podcast. Other people got to see how funny Robert is. My kids love to send Robert Greene books like “Does It Fart?” and “I Need a New Butt” because they know he’ll love them. It reminds me of the contrast between Heraclitus and Democritus. One, understanding the darkness of the world, would cry. The other, understanding the darkness of the world, would laugh. Which would you rather be?

– Get comfortable with contradiction. People will sometimes email me, “Ryan, Marcus Aurelius contradicts himself. Sometimes he says to zoom in and other times he says to zoom out.” Or they’ll point out that Seneca’s writings tell us to be aware of the dangers of the future and also never avoid anxiety and worry.” Or that they are confused because Law 3 in Robert’s The 48 Laws of Power is “conceal your intentions” but Law 6 is “court attention at all cost.” Isn’t that a contradiction? The answer is yes. Yes, the Stoics contradict themselves. Yes, Robert’s laws of power contradict each other. Yes, I contradict myself. Because the world is complicated, ambiguous, paradoxical, and contradictory. Because different situations call for different things. Because everything in life depends on context. As F. Scott Fitzgerald famously wrote, “The test of a first-rate intelligence is the ability to hold two opposing ideas in mind at the same time and still retain the ability to function.”

– Having a physical practice is essential to the creative life. It was Robert who first got me hooked on swimming in 2007. I had grown up swimming but had drifted toward running. Robert recommended the Los Angeles Athletic Club, and swimming became part of my life again. I learned from his commitment to it, from the value of time when there was no phone, no conversation, no new information to take in. Some days, it turns it off in a very restorative way. Other days, it lets it wander and work on things. I’ve gotten over grudges. I’ve calmed down. I’ve gotten much-needed space. The temptation under pressure is to eliminate these breaks. But the hours at the desk aren’t the only hours that contribute to the work.

– Be generous with credit. It’s funny, Robert talked about “never outshining the master” and “let others do all the work but take all the credit” in The 48 Laws of Power, yet in reality, he’s generous, patient and supportive. No one has helped me more in my career. I’m sure it’s obnoxious for him to be asked about me in interviews but he never gets frustrated. There’s no way I can repay Robert for his kindness and his patience and his generosity. The only thing I can do is pay it forward.

– “It’s all material,” Robert likes to say. Everything that happens in your life can be used for something useful, whether it’s your writing, your relationships, or your new startup. In the introduction to The Law of the Sublime, Robert describes working on the book after his 2018 stroke. His left hand was frozen. He could no longer type as before and would have to essentially write and edit the manuscript by hand. He could no longer take the hikes that had helped him work through his other books. Originally, he had imagined traveling down the Amazon, encountering chimpanzees in Africa, having extraordinary experiences to write about. Now he could barely get out the front door. “Now my small backyard would have to be my Amazon jungle,” he writes. He began looking at the lizards, squirrels, and hummingbirds. His limitations changed the book. He had to find the sublime in the simplest things—and show readers that they could find it without traveling anywhere or undertaking some great adventure. These obstacles become opportunities. If you start asking more often, “How can I use this to my advantage?”—your creative output will not only get better, your life will too.

– Savor this incredibly rare experience we’ve been granted. Near the end of The Law of the Sublime, Robert writes, “You who are reading this are a current member of the Club of the Living. One by one, all around you and all over the world, people are permanently leaving the Club.” When Robert first taught me about alive time, I thought about it mostly as something that gives you urgency and makes you more productive. As I’ve gotten older, I’ve come to understand what it really does is give you the present moment and make you more appreciative. Of the banal, the mundane, the everyday. The soft paw prints on the dusty trunk of a car, the feeling of a pen gliding across a notecard, the sounds of birds, the subtle shifts of light through the windows—this is what Robert means by the sublime. “That we have been granted this incredibly rare conscious experience of our mysterious universe,” he writes, “no matter how briefly, should fill us with continuous awe.” Sit in awe of existence. Let the rareness of this experience wash over you. Be present for it. Savor it—this brief time we get as members of the Club of the Living.

– Memento mori. We almost lost Robert in 2018, when he suffered his stroke. The people we depend on, the people we learn from, the people we assume we’ll always be able to call—you think there will always be another conversation. Another chance to ask that question. Another opportunity to tell them what they’ve meant to you. But none of that is guaranteed. I’m grateful Robert is still here, still writing, still teaching me. I don’t want to take that for granted. It has been one of the great perks of my life to be able to pick up the phone and ask him for advice. But I don’t get an unlimited number of those calls. None of us gets unlimited time with the people who have shaped our lives. Pick up the phone, send the note, make the trip—tell them what they mean to you, while you still can.
